description: Pop Art responds to the consumer society. **Warhol** and **Lichtenstein** make advertising, comics and stars great art.

hero.hook: A can of soup, a box of comic books: what if the banal was the icon of the century?

blocks.text: **Pop Art**, from the mid-**1950** to the **1970**, responds to  and mass culture. Advertising, comics, Hollywood stars: everything becomes material for art. [[American consumer society of the 1950s and 60s]]

With **Andy Warhol** and **Roy Lichtenstein**, the line blurs between the museum and the supermarket. The everyday object becomes an icon. The value of the work and the role of the artist are disrupted.

Pop Art was born in **Great Britain** with , but it was in the **United States**, in the years **1960**, that it exploded. Post-war, prosperity, supermarkets, logos everywhere: the visual landscape of Americans has changed. [[Independent Group]]
In 1957, Richard Hamilton defined Pop Art with adjectives: “ephemeral”, “cheap”, “sexy”. An art to consume as quickly as a magazine.

Pop artists opposed the [[Abstract Expressionism]], these introspective paintings then dominant. When Warhol paints soups, he shows that the individual is defined by what he buys. Repetition drains the image of its emotion, leaving only its commercial effectiveness.

sections.title: From everyday life to the museum

blocks.text: **Andy Warhol** (1928-1987), former advertising graphic designer, applies industry methods to art. His **Factory**, in New York, is no longer a solitary sanctuary: assistants and friends produce together.

blocks.caption: Marilyn in series: the star as a reproducible product.

blocks.text: Warhol accumulated more than 600 “time capsules”: boxes where he threw letters, bills and even leftover food.

His queen technique: , which allows an image to be reproduced dozens of times. By multiplying Marilyn Monroe, he illustrates the idea of ​​: the more the image circulates, the less “sacred” it is, the more it becomes an icon. Fame itself is a product. [[Screen printing]] [[Aura and mechanized reproduction (Walter Benjamin)]]
**Roy Lichtenstein** (1923-1997) attacks the language of **comics**. He isolates a box loaded with emotional cliché and paints it in monumental format.

blocks.caption: Hand-painted Ben-Day dots: the factory imitated by gesture.

blocks.text: To judge a composition, Lichtenstein looked at his paintings upside down in a mirror, to see if they held up in a purely abstract way.

Its signature: the [[Ben-Day]] point, these small industrial printing dots which create nuances. He paints them by hand with stencils: hours to imitate what a machine does in seconds. *Whaam!* transforms a diversion box into a modern history painting.

Pop Art changes the market and institutions. The artist's mark matters as much as the gesture. In **2022**, a portrait of Marilyn by Warhol reached **195 million** dollars: the mass image, sacralized, becomes the most precious commodity.

blocks.text: Warhol’s prediction of “15 minutes of fame” has become our digital daily life. Memes and image recycling are a direct result of this revolution.
Pop Art broke the barrier between high art and mass culture. Through screen printing and Ben-Day dots, Warhol and Lichtenstein turned everyday objects and stars into lasting icons.
